evidence: Traupman 409: what’s wrong with you?, quid est tibi? or quid est tēcum?
Plaut. Curc. 236: sed quid tibi est?

terms.comment: Literally “what of a matter is it?”. Not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections in this form; Traupman is the only evidence.

terms.gloss: what is it? what’s the matter?
terms.comment: The plain answer to being called or to a worried face; Quid tibi est? asks what is wrong with the person.

evidence: Traupman 103: what on earth’s the matter?, quidnam est?
terms.comment: -nam makes the question urgent or surprised.

evidence: Liv. 3.48.4: quid hoc reī sit (Lewis & Short s.v. percontor)
terms.comment: The partitive genitive reī with a neuter pronoun, as Livy asks quid hoc reī sit, “what this is all about”; Plautus builds quid istuc est verbī? the same way (Plaut. Curc. 1.1.32). The exact words are Traupman’s.

In Plautus quid jam? is “why so? how so?” and is answered with quia (Plaut. Mil. 2.3.51, Lewis & Short s.v. luscitiōsus; see why so?). For what is wrong, Quid tibi est? (above) or Quid istuc malī est? (see trouble).

phrases.english: “What’s the matter? Do your ears hurt?”

phrases.latin: quid agis? — Vīvō. — Nempe ut dignus es. sed quid tibi est?
phrases.english: How are you? — Alive. — As you deserve, no doubt. But what’s wrong with you?

phrases.latin: Dāve. — Hem, quid est? — Ehodum ad mē!
phrases.english: Davus! — Eh, what is it? — Come here to me!

phrases.latin: Hem tibi autem. — Quidnam est? — Lupus in fābulā.
phrases.english: Look out! — What on earth is it? — Speak of the devil.
